opus-5.5.text:
I think the main lesson I've drawn is that we should be a lot more careful about the difference between a commitment and an aspiration, and honest about which one we're actually making.

When a lot of these safety frameworks were first being written, there was a sense that the way to make them meaningful was to make them sound binding: "If we see capability X, we will not proceed until we have protection Y." That has real appeal. It gives people something concrete to hold you to. But the world is messy. You don't know in advance exactly what the risks will look like, what mitigations will be feasible, or what your competitors will be doing. So you can end up in a spot where the commitment, read literally, says one thing, and your honest judgment about what's best for safety says another. That's a really bad place to be, for a couple of reasons.

First, it creates pressure to quietly reinterpret things. You start parsing the language, deciding that some threshold wasn't "really" crossed, or that a mitigation "basically" counts. That erodes trust, and it erodes the internal culture too. People learn that the document is something you lawyer around rather than something you take seriously.

Second, if you're unilaterally committing to pause or slow down in situations where others won't, you might just be handing the frontier to less careful actors. I don't think that's an excuse for anything goes, but it's a real consideration, and pretending it isn't doesn't help.

So what I'd rather see, and what I've come to advocate, is something more like: be very explicit about what you're confident you can actually stick to, and frame the rest honestly as your current plan or your best guess at what good practice looks like. Pair that with transparency. Tell people what risks you're seeing, what you're doing about them, and where you're falling short of what you'd ideally want. If you have to change course, say so loudly and explain why, rather than letting it happen through quiet edits.

The bigger lesson is that voluntary company commitments can only carry so much weight. They're useful for developing ideas, building norms, and showing what's feasible, a kind of testing ground for what regulation might eventually look like. But if the hope was that companies would lock themselves into strict unilateral constraints and that would be enough, I think that was always going to strain against competitive reality. The things that really bind everyone tend to need to be shared: industry-wide standards, government requirements, verification. Company policies are a stepping stone toward that, not a substitute.

And one more thing. I'd rather a company say "here's an honest picture of where we are and what we're struggling with" than make a beautiful promise it later breaks. Credibility is a resource we're going to need a lot of later, when the stakes are higher. Spending it on commitments that don't hold is a bad trade.

r001.rationale: It recommends being explicit about what companies can honor, reframing the rest as plans or best guesses, and openly explaining changes when commitments no longer fit.

r002.rationale: It does not mention METR or say that revising commitments proved more painful than Holden Karnofsky and METR had anticipated.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the big lesson for me is that there's a real difference between a commitment that's shaped like a promise and a commitment that's shaped like a plan. A lot of the early safety commitments in this space were written when nobody really knew what the frontier was going to look like, how fast competitors would move, or what the actual technical difficulty of some of these evaluations and mitigations would turn out to be. So companies said things like, "We won't deploy a model above capability X until we have safeguard Y," and that sounds great, but if safeguard Y turns out to be a genuinely unsolved research problem, you've put yourself in a position where the choice is between walking back the commitment publicly or quietly reinterpreting it. Neither of those is good for trust.

The lesson I'd draw isn't that companies shouldn't make commitments. It's that we should be a lot more careful about what kind of commitment we're asking for. I've become much more interested in commitments to process and transparency than commitments to specific outcomes. "We will run these evaluations, we will publish the results, we will say in advance what we'd consider alarming, and if we change our thresholds we'll explain why" — that's something a company can actually keep, even in a world where the technology surprises them. Whereas "we will never do X" is a bet about the future, and companies are structurally bad at keeping bets about the future when there's enormous commercial pressure pushing the other way.

The other thing I'd say is that I've updated toward thinking voluntary commitments are a weak foundation on their own. They're useful as a way of surfacing what the right norms are, and as a kind of scaffolding for what regulation might eventually look like. But if the only thing holding a line is a company's own word, and the company is in a race, you should expect that line to move. That's not a cynical take about any particular lab, it's just what incentives do. So I think the honest response to seeing commitments get softened is not to be shocked, but to say: this tells us we need external verification, we need third parties who can check the claims, and we need something with teeth behind it eventually. The commitments were a first draft, and watching them bend under pressure is actually informative about which parts of the draft were never realistic.

r001.rationale: The response favors process and transparency commitments over promises about outcomes, but does not clearly recommend revising commitments that do not make sense.

r002.rationale: It does not say that revising commitments was more painful than Holden Karnofsky and METR had anticipated.

astra-6.text:
I think the lesson is that a commitment is only as useful as your willingness to stick to it when it becomes costly. It’s easy to say, “We’ll stop if things look dangerous,” when stopping is a hypothetical. It’s much harder when you’re looking at a particular decision and you believe your competitors are going to keep going.

That doesn’t mean commitments are useless. It means we should ask more concrete questions: Who decides whether the threshold has been crossed? What information will they have? What happens if the company can’t meet the conditions it laid out? And is the consequence actually to pause, or is it to revise the conditions?

I’d also distinguish learning that a particular safety test was poorly designed from finding that a commitment is inconvenient. You want room to improve the tests as you learn. But if commercial pressure is enough to change the promise, then the promise wasn’t providing the protection people thought it was. Ultimately, I don’t think we should expect voluntary commitments alone to carry that burden.

r001.rationale: The response allows improving poorly designed safety tests, but does not recommend revising commitments that do not make sense.

r002.rationale: It does not say that revising commitments proved more painful than Karnofsky and METR had anticipated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the lesson is that a safety commitment is most useful when it makes the tradeoff explicit in advance. If you’re saying, “We’ll do this unless it becomes really costly or puts us at a competitive disadvantage,” then you haven’t necessarily committed to very much. Those are precisely the circumstances in which you need the commitment to matter.

That doesn’t mean a company should promise things it can’t deliver, or that a policy should never change. You learn things; circumstances change. But I’d like to see companies spell out what evidence would trigger a pause, who has the authority to make that call, and what happens if they can’t implement the safeguards they’ve said are necessary. And if they change those conditions, that should be visible and explained.

So my takeaway is to put less weight on the existence of a commitment and more weight on whether there’s a credible process for sticking to it when doing so is painful.

r001.rationale: The response allows that policies may change and says changes should be explained, but it does not recommend revising commitments specifically when they no longer make sense.

r002.rationale: It does not say that revising commitments proved more painful than Holden Karnofsky and METR had anticipated.
